catalog_quote: There is one primary stress per phonological word (see 2.7) and stress rules operate with reference to the syllable. A final syllable receives primary stress if it is a closed syllable; if the final syllable is an open syllable, the primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, that is, stress falls on the last vowel that is followed by a consonant. ma.la.lúm (closed last syllable) 'soft' má.la (open last syllable) 'hawk' ... The stress pattern in the language is similar to many Oceanic languages where primary stress most commonly falls on the penultimate syllable. Where additional syllables are added to a word through affixation or cliticisation, the stress moves to accommodate this and the rules above still apply: βí.ti 'tell' βi.tí.a 'tell him/her/it' ... Light secondary stress falls on the second syllable preceding the penultimate syllable where a phonological word is more than …

The classification (weight-sensitive, right edge: final stress iff final syllable closed by N, else penult; secondary two syllables before the penult) matches the source exactly. 258). sources.citation: Riehl, Anastasia K. & Dorothy Jauncey. 2005. Tamambo. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 35(2): 255-259. DOI 10.1017/S0025100305002197 (Illustrations of the IPA, open on Cambridge Core).
sources.quote: "Stress falls on the penultimate syllable, except when the final syllable is closed, in which case stress is ultimate. Phonetically, stressed syllables tend to be longer than their unstressed counterparts, with both the syllable onset consonant and vowel exhibiting increased duration." Also notes question intonation peaks on the antepenult then falls on 'the penultimate (usually stressed) syllable', and that fast-speech /u/-deletion can shift which syllable surfaces as stressed (["momle] < /mo-mule/).
sources.note: JIPA Illustration with a Prosody paragraph and a phonetic cue statement (duration) for stress; independent restatement of the closed-final-else-penult rule our 'weight' coding rests on. downloaded now; confirms.
